items.explanation: Small-town America backed Prohibition, immigration restriction, and deporting radicals — but it demanded creationism in schools (the Scopes trial), not opposed it.
options: A. Increase immigration from Eastern Europe
B. Require teaching creationism in schools
C. Ease penalties for bootleggers
D. Make deporting suspected radicals harder
items.stem: Rural and small-town America in the 1920s would support legislation to

option_explanations.A: Small-town America did not support increasing immigration from Eastern Europe — it backed the 1921 and 1924 restriction acts that choked it off. Rural voters wanted fewer immigrants, not more.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Rural and small-town America in the 1920s backed Prohibition, immigration restriction, and deporting suspected radicals — and it demanded creationism in public schools, the impulse behind the 1925 Scopes trial.
option_explanations.C: Rural America did not want easier penalties for bootleggers — it supported Prohibition and wanted it enforced. Bootleggers were the enemy of dry America, not its protégés.
option_explanations.D: Rural America wanted deporting suspected radicals to be easier, not harder — the Red Scare and the Palmer Raids had strong small-town support.

items.explanation: Bruce Barton's The Man Nobody Knows (1925) recast Jesus as a master salesman and businessman — the decade's definitive celebration of commerce, unlike Lewis's satires or Fitzgerald's critique.
options: A. Main Street
B. The Great Gatsby
C. The Man Nobody Knows
D. Babbitt
items.stem: The novel that most fully endorsed 1920s business philosophy was

option_explanations.A: Main Street (1920) satirized small-town life and its boosterism — Sinclair Lewis mocked the business mentality, he did not endorse it.
option_explanations.B: The Great Gatsby (1925) critiqued the hollowness of Jazz Age wealth — Fitzgerald exposed the emptiness behind the glitter, not a celebration of business philosophy.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Bruce Barton's The Man Nobody Knows (1925) recast Jesus as a master salesman and businessman — a direct celebration of commerce and advertising, the decade's definitive endorsement of business philosophy.
option_explanations.D: Babbitt (1922) satirized the conformist businessman — Lewis held George Babbitt up for ridicule, not admiration.

items.explanation: Prohibition made the speakeasy the urban institution of the decade; immigration had been choked by the 1921 and 1924 acts, the Klan's strength lay outside eastern cities, and bread lines belonged to the 1930s.
options: A. A speakeasy
B. A steady stream of European immigrants
C. Massed Ku Klux Klan supporters
D. The first bread lines
items.stem: In 1928, in most Eastern cities, one could find

option_explanations.A: Correct. Prohibition made the speakeasy the urban institution of the decade — illegal bars flourished in every Eastern city by 1928.
option_explanations.B: European immigration had been choked off by the 1921 and 1924 restriction acts — the steady stream of immigrants belonged to the prewar era, not 1928.
option_explanations.C: The Ku Klux Klan's strength in the 1920s lay in the South, the Midwest, and small towns — not massed in Eastern cities, where the Klan was politically weak.
option_explanations.D: Bread lines belonged to the 1930s Depression. In 1928 the country was still in the midst of apparent prosperity; the bread lines came after the 1929 crash.

items.explanation: Republican orthodoxy held that government's business was business, that Washington should do little, and that immigration should stay restricted — but strengthening unions was never on the agenda.
options: A. 'The business of government is business'
B. Government should do as little as possible
C. Labor unions should be strengthened by law
D. Immigration should remain restricted
items.stem: Republican leaders of the 1920s believed all of the following EXCEPT

option_explanations.A: Coolidge's 'the business of government is business' really was Republican orthodoxy — this was a genuine belief of 1920s Republican leaders, not the exception.
option_explanations.B: Republican leaders really did believe government should do as little as possible — laissez-faire was their governing creed. This is not the exception.
option_explanations.C: Correct — this is the exception. Strengthening labor unions by law was never on the Republican agenda; the 1920s Republicans favored open shops and used injunctions against strikers, not pro-union legislation.
option_explanations.D: Republican leaders really did believe immigration should remain restricted — the 1924 act was their work and they defended it. This is not the exception.

items.explanation: Hoover's landslide showed faith in Republican prosperity, the salience of Prohibition, and anti-Catholic resistance to Al Smith — but it did not heal the urban-rural divide, which yawned wider than ever.
options: A. Voters credited Republicans for prosperity
B. Urban-rural divisions had faded
C. Prohibition remained a hot-button issue
D. America rejected a Catholic candidate
items.stem: Hoover's 1928 election demonstrated all of the following EXCEPT

option_explanations.A: Voters really did credit Republicans for prosperity in 1928 — 'a chicken in every pot' Hoover ran on continued Republican good times. This was demonstrated by the election, not the exception.
option_explanations.B: Correct — this is the exception. The urban-rural divide did not fade in 1928 — it yawned wider than ever, with Smith carrying the big cities and Hoover sweeping the countryside. The election exposed the split, it did not heal it.
option_explanations.C: Prohibition really did remain a hot-button issue in 1928 — Smith was wet, Hoover dry, and the issue divided voters sharply. This was demonstrated, not the exception.
option_explanations.D: America really did reject a Catholic candidate in 1928 — anti-Catholic prejudice hurt Al Smith badly, especially in the South and Midwest. This was demonstrated, not the exception.

items.explanation: Parker never engages McPherson's theology; she performs a witty execution -- 'were you to call it a little peach, you would not be so much as scratching its surface,' capped by the deadpan 'the Statue of Liberty is situated in Lake Ontario.' The review is a demolition of celebrity self-promotion in Parker's signature ironic voice.
options: A. A witty demolition of celebrity self-promotion
B. An earnest endorsement of McPherson's ministry
C. A theological defense of religious fundamentalism
D. A neutral summary of the book's plot
items.stem: Parker's review of McPherson's autobiography is best described as
items.stimulus:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

Reviewing Aimee Semple McPherson's autobiography, Dorothy Parker archly treats the celebrity evangelist's book as show business — entertaining, sensational, and revealing how thoroughly religion, like everything else in the 1920s, had become a form of mass entertainment.
—After Dorothy Parker's review of McPherson's This Is That, 1920s

option_explanations.A: Correct. Parker never engages McPherson's theology; she performs a witty execution of the celebrity evangelist's self-promotion — treating the autobiography as show business, entertaining and sensational, in her signature ironic voice.
option_explanations.B: Parker did not endorse McPherson's ministry — her review is arch and mocking, treating the book as entertainment, not as a spiritual work to be recommended.
option_explanations.C: Parker mounted no theological defense of fundamentalism — she never engages theology at all. The review is about celebrity and show business, not doctrine.
option_explanations.D: The review is not a neutral summary of the plot — it is a pointed, witty demolition. Parker editorializes throughout rather than summarizing neutrally.

items.explanation: McPherson built her International Church of the Foursquare Gospel on radio broadcasts and theatrical stagecraft -- Parker dubs her 'Our Lady of the Loudspeaker.' New mass media let a preacher become a national celebrity, a distinctly 1920s phenomenon; it marked revivalism's adaptation to modernity, not religion's decline or women's retreat.
options: A. The decline of all religious observance in America
B. The triumph of mainline churches over revivalism
C. The end of women's public religious roles
D. The rise of mass media that turned preachers into celebrities
items.stem: McPherson's national prominence illustrates which 1920s development?
items.stimulus:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

Reviewing Aimee Semple McPherson's autobiography, Dorothy Parker archly treats the celebrity evangelist's book as show business — entertaining, sensational, and revealing how thoroughly religion, like everything else in the 1920s, had become a form of mass entertainment.
—After Dorothy Parker's review of McPherson's This Is That, 1920s

option_explanations.A: Religious observance did not decline across the board in the 1920s — revivalism thrived. McPherson's prominence shows religion adapting to mass media, not dying.
option_explanations.B: Mainline churches did not triumph over revivalism in the 1920s — McPherson's Foursquare Gospel was revivalism at its most theatrical and successful.
option_explanations.C: Women's public religious roles did not end — McPherson herself, a woman leading a national ministry, proves the opposite.
option_explanations.D: Correct. McPherson built her International Church of the Foursquare Gospel on radio broadcasts and theatrical stagecraft — 'Our Lady of the Loudspeaker.' New mass media let a preacher become a national celebrity, a distinctly 1920s development.

items.explanation: The 'Lost Generation' -- Hemingway, Fitzgerald, Dos Passos -- fled to Paris, where Gertrude Stein's salon became their headquarters. Exile was itself the critique: they found the prosperous America Parker satirized spiritually empty and went abroad to write about it.
options: A. they joined the Communist Party in large numbers
B. they abandoned literature for electoral politics
C. they moved to Paris and wrote as expatriates
D. they emigrated to the Soviet Union
items.stem: Many American writers of the 1920s, disillusioned with American life, responded by

The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

Reviewing Aimee Semple McPherson's autobiography, Dorothy Parker archly treats the celebrity evangelist's book as show business — entertaining, sensational, and revealing how thoroughly religion, like everything else in the 1920s, had become a form of mass entertainment.
—After Dorothy Parker's review of McPherson's This Is That, 1920s

option_explanations.A: American writers did not join the Communist Party in large numbers in the 1920s. The characteristic response of the disillusioned was exile, not party membership.
option_explanations.B: They did not abandon literature for electoral politics — they kept writing. Their response was to write from abroad, not to run for office.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The 'Lost Generation' — Hemingway, Fitzgerald, Dos Passos — moved to Paris, where Gertrude Stein's salon became their headquarters. Exile was itself the critique: they found prosperous America spiritually empty and went abroad to write about it.
option_explanations.D: They did not emigrate to the Soviet Union — their chosen exile was Paris, not Moscow. The Lost Generation's destination was literary Paris.
